Chapter 1

Embracing the Unknown

拥抱未知

It’s essential to know what you’re up against when trying to lead in a chaotic environment. Understanding the nature and extent of the chaos is crucial for effective leadership, as it enables you to identify the root causes of dysfunction and address them strategically. This awareness helps you to navigate challenges more effectively, prioritize critical issues, and implement solutions to restore order and drive progress.

在混乱的环境中带团队，首先必须清楚自己面对的是什么。理解混乱的本质与范围，对于有效领导至关重要——它能帮你找出功能失调的根因，并策略性地加以应对。这种认知让你更从容地应对挑战、把关键问题排到优先级前面，并通过落地解决方案来恢复秩序、推动进展。

What Does Chaos Look Like?

混乱是什么样子？

Sometimes, it can be hard to tell whether your organization is chaotic or if there’s just some fuzziness around the edges. Chaos can become a creeping normality. There’s a fable about boiling frogs: a frog placed in boiling water will immediately jump out, but if placed in tepid water and heated gradually, it won’t perceive the danger and will boil to death. That fable, while factually incorrect, has parallels for how chaos can creep up within an organization.

有时候很难分辨：你的组织到底是真的混乱，还是只是边缘有点模糊。混乱会像慢性病一样悄悄变成“新常态”。有个“温水煮青蛙”的寓言：把青蛙丢进开水里，它会立刻跳出来；但如果放进温水里慢慢加热，它察觉不到危险，最终被煮死。这个寓言虽然在生物学上并不成立，却很贴切地描述了混乱如何在一个组织里悄然蔓延。

Your ability to assess the level of chaos can also be variable, especially when starting a new role. In these situations, sometimes you know what you’re getting yourself into; your new employer has been transparent about their issues. But sometimes the challenges are presented to you in a rosier light than is really the case. Indeed, you’ve probably interviewed for a new job in a new environment; you put your best foot forward, and the company, in turn, tried to sell you on their mission, product, and culture. But lo and behold, when you start, you discover challenges and chaos existing that you did not expect.

你对混乱程度的判断能力也会波动，尤其是刚接手一个新岗位时。这种情况下，有时你清楚自己要面对什么——新雇主对自己的问题很坦诚；但有时，挑战被包装得比实际情况光鲜得多。说起来，你自己面试新工作时大概也是这样：你尽力展现最好的一面，公司则反过来向你推销它的使命、产品和文化。可一旦入职你就会发现，现实里到处都是意料之外的挑战与混乱。

Even if you’re already part of an organization, chaos can sometimes be more evident from different perspectives. James once worked in a large corporate environment where several teams were functional because their leaders shielded them from the broader organization’s dysfunction. The organization’s state was revealed more accurately when James was promoted to leadership level.

即便你早已身在某个组织之中，换个视角有时也会让混乱变得格外刺眼。James 曾在一家大型企业工作，当时有几个团队看起来运转良好，因为团队领导把他们和整个组织的功能失调隔离开了。等到 James 自己被提拔到领导岗，才更真实地看清这家组织到底是什么状态。

— 原书第 21 页 —

Understanding the symptoms and behaviors in chaotic environments can also be helpful, even if you know things are chaotic—especially if you’re going to develop strategies to work through, over, around, or under that chaos.

即便你已经知道局面很混乱，去识别混乱环境中的典型症状与行为模式仍然很有帮助——尤其是当你要制定策略，去穿透、跨越、绕开或者钻过这片混乱时。

Chaos can manifest in many ways within an organization. Some common symptoms include the following:

混乱在组织中会以多种形式表现出来。常见的症状包括：

  • Lack of ownership

    缺乏主人翁意识

  • Absence of structure

    组织结构缺失

  • Outsized responsibility

    责任与角色不匹配（责任过重）

  • Undefined processes

    流程不明确

  • Poor communication

    沟通不畅

  • Blame culture, scapegoating, and recrimination

    指责文化、找替罪羊与互相归咎

  • High turnover

    高离职率

  • Lack of strategy and planning

    缺乏战略与规划

  • Frequent crisis mode

    频繁进入危机模式

  • No meaningful measurement

    缺乏有意义的度量

Let’s dive deeper into some of these areas.

下面我们挑其中几个方面展开细说。

Lack of Ownership

缺乏主人翁意识

In a chaotic environment, it is often unclear who is responsible for what. This ambiguity gives rise to a range of problems. Tasks and decisions can easily fall through the cracks because no one is clearly accountable for them. Confusion and delays are common; either people assume someone else is handling a task, or multiple individuals might redundantly attempt to tackle the same issue.

在混乱的环境里，常常说不清谁该为什么负责。这种模糊会引发一系列问题：任务和决策很容易掉进缝隙，因为没有人被明确问责。混乱与拖延随处可见——要么大家以为别人在做某件事，要么好几个人重复地去解决同一个问题。

This lack of ownership makes it difficult to resolve issues or implement improvements. Without clear responsibility, it’s easy for things to devolve into a blame game or a state of learned helplessness where everyone waits for someone else to step up and take action.

这种主人翁意识的缺失，让解决问题、推动改进都变得困难。责任不清时，事情很容易退化成互相甩锅，或者陷入“习得性无助”——每个人都在等别人先站出来采取行动。

Absence of Structure

组织结构缺失

Closely related to the lack of ownership is a lack of organizational structure. In a chaotic environment, teams and roles are often poorly defined. Individuals often struggle to understand their place within the broader context and the impact of their work on overall goals. This lack of structure makes collaboration and decision making extremely difficult. Without clear lanes, teams often duplicate effort or work at cross-purposes. The left hand doesn’t know what the right is doing, leading to wasted resources and conflict.

与缺乏主人翁意识紧密相关的，是组织结构的缺失。在混乱的环境里，团队和角色往往界定不清，个人很难理解自己在大局中的位置，也看不清自己的工作对整体目标有什么影响。这种结构缺失让协作与决策变得极其困难：没有清晰的分工赛道，团队之间常常重复劳动，甚至互相掣肘；左手不知道右手在做什么，结果就是资源浪费和冲突。

— 原书第 22 页 —

Outsized Responsibility

责任过重

When ownership and structure are lacking, it’s common for individuals to assume outsized responsibility relative to their role or level of experience. A junior engineer might find themselves as the sole owner of a critical system. A manager might be responsible for multiple teams and products without sufficient resources or support.

当主人翁意识和组织结构都缺位时，个人常常会承担起与自己的角色、经验级别不相称的过重责任。一个初级工程师可能发现自己成了某个关键系统的唯一负责人；一个经理可能在资源和支持都不足的情况下，同时扛着好几个团队和产品线。

This situation is a recipe for burnout. Individuals are stretched too thin and lack the experience or authority to handle their responsibilities effectively. It also creates significant risk for the organization, as a single person becomes a bottleneck or single point of failure.

这种局面几乎注定会导致倦怠。个人被摊得太薄，既缺乏相应经验、也没有相应权限去有效地履行职责。对组织来说这也是巨大风险——单个人变成了瓶颈，或者说单点故障。

Undefined Process

流程不明确

In chaotic organizations, processes are often made up on the fly or exist only as institutional knowledge. Documentation is lacking, and the way work gets done is inconsistent and unreliable.

在混乱的组织里，流程常常是临时拍脑袋定出来的，或者只存在于老员工的脑子里。文档匮乏，做事的方式既不一致也不可靠。

These gaps make it extremely difficult to onboard new team members. Without transparent processes to follow, new hires struggle to become productive contributors. It also means that the organization often reinvents the wheel, with each team or individual creating their own way of doing things.

这些缺口让新人上手变得极其困难。没有透明可遵循的流程，新员工很难成长为能产出的人。这也意味着组织经常在重复造轮子——每个团队、每个人都在自创一套做事方式。

This lack of process creates resistance to change and stifles innovation. People cling to what they know “works,” even if it’s suboptimal, because change introduces the risk of failure. Turning inward and being insular also breeds a culture of “not invented here,” where the organization aggressively rejects external innovation.

流程缺失还会催生对变革的抵触、扼杀创新。人们死死抱住自己“知道能用”的做法，哪怕它并不理想——因为改变意味着失败的风险。这种向内收缩、自我封闭的心态还会滋生“非我所创”（not invented here）的文化：组织会本能地排斥外部的一切创新。

We know this sounds contradictory. Indeed, how can a chaotic organization—where nothing is stable and things change minute by minute—also be risk-averse and resistant to innovation? People become accustomed to their situations. The chaos becomes predictable. We’ve both had situations where people have reached a state of fatalistic acceptance of their organizational chaos—or even worse, they believe any change will only deepen the dysfunction. Attempts to address that chaos must defeat both this fatalism and the underlying causes of the chaos.1

我们知道这听起来矛盾：一个什么都不稳定、每分钟都在变的混乱组织，怎么会同时厌恶风险、抗拒创新呢？因为人们会逐渐习惯自己的处境，混乱反而变得“可预测”。我们俩都遇到过这样的情况：团队成员对组织的混乱达到了一种认命式的接受——甚至更糟，他们相信任何改变只会让功能失调更严重。想要解决混乱，就必须同时战胜这种宿命论和混乱背后的根因。1

1 Albeit, sometimes chaos and fatalism are self-reinforcing: there is chaos, so we become fatalistic, which in turn generates more chaos.

1 不过，有时混乱与宿命论会互相强化：因为混乱，我们变得认命；认命又反过来制造更多混乱。

Without a clear and safe way to evolve processes, the organization stagnates.

如果没有一条清晰、安全的路径去迭代流程，组织就会停滞不前。

— 原书第 23 页 —

Poor Communication

沟通不畅

Communication breakdowns are common in chaotic organizations. Information often becomes siloed within teams and isn’t effectively shared. Updates and decisions are communicated haphazardly, if at all, and relevant stakeholders are left out of key conversations.

在混乱的组织里，沟通断裂很常见。信息往往被封闭在各个团队内部，得不到有效共享；进展更新和决策即便传达也是杂乱无章，相关利益方常常被排除在关键讨论之外。

Sometimes, there is an active effort in chaotic organizations to restrict communication—either because “no news is good news” or because communicating the current state can make you or your team a target of blame or recrimination.

有时，混乱组织里甚至会主动限制沟通——要么是信奉“没有消息就是好消息”，要么是因为如实汇报现状，会让你或你的团队成为被指责、被归咎的靶子。

This effort leads to people feeling out of the loop and disconnected from the bigger picture. It breeds confusion, resentment, anger, and a lack of alignment. Like the lack of structure, this also results in duplicated effort and teams working at cross-purposes.

这种做法会让大家感觉被排除在外、与大局脱节，滋生困惑、怨恨、愤怒和方向不一致。和结构缺失一样，它同样会导致重复劳动和团队之间互相拧巴。

Blame Culture, Scapegoating, and Recrimination

指责文化、找替罪羊与互相归咎

In a chaotic organization, a blame culture often prevails. This manifests as individuals or teams looking for someone to blame when things go wrong rather than focusing on solving the problem. This culture discourages risk-taking and innovation, as employees fear the repercussions of failure.

在混乱的组织里，指责文化往往占上风。出了问题时，个人或团队第一反应是找人来背锅，而不是聚焦于解决问题。这种文化会压抑冒险精神和创新，因为员工害怕失败带来的后果。

Blame culture creates an environment of fear where employees are reluctant to take ownership of their work or make decisions. This hesitancy can lead to stagnation and a lack of progress; individuals become more focused on avoiding blame than contributing positively to the organization’s goals. Over time, this will significantly erode trust and morale within the team.

指责文化制造出一种恐惧氛围：员工不愿对工作负责，也不愿做决策。这种犹豫会导致停滞不前——大家更关心如何别被怪罪，而不是如何为组织目标做贡献。长此以往，团队内部的信任和士气会被严重侵蚀。

James worked in an environment where, before any attempt to resolve an incident, there was a cycle of “whose fault is it?” One of his colleagues coined the term “blamestorm” to describe the incident-management process. Repeatedly, these efforts to assign blame added significant delays to the recovery time. In turn, this led to conflict and friction among internal teams, external vendors, and leadership.

James 曾在这样一个环境里工作：每次还没开始解决事故，先来一轮“这是谁的锅？”。他的一位同事甚至造了个词——“甩锅风暴”（blamestorm）——来形容这套事故管理流程。一次又一次，这些互相追责的动作大幅拉长了恢复时间，还在内部团队、外部供应商和领导层之间制造了冲突与摩擦。

Scapegoating is another symptom in which individuals or teams are unfairly blamed for systemic problems. This can lead to high turnover, low morale, and a toxic work environment in which employees prioritize self-preservation over collaboration and progress.

找替罪羊是另一种症状：系统性问题被不公平地怪到某个个人或团队头上。这会导致高离职率、低士气，以及一种有毒的工作环境——员工把自我保护看得比协作和进展更重要。

Scapegoating fosters a hostile work environment where collaboration is stifled and fear prevails. It diverts attention from addressing the root causes of issues and instead creates an atmosphere of mistrust and division. Employees may become disengaged and disconnected from the organization’s mission, exacerbating the chaos.

找替罪羊会助长充满敌意的工作氛围：协作被压制，恐惧主导一切。它把注意力从解决问题根因上移开，制造出互不信任、相互割裂的气氛。员工可能逐渐离心离德，与组织的使命脱节，反而让混乱雪上加霜。

Ultimately, this results in recrimination, characterized by retaliatory accusations and back-and-forth blame exchanges. This hampers effective problem-solving and deteriorates trust among team members and across departments, further entrenching chaos. Recrimination can create a cycle of negativity that is hard to break. It often leads to a toxic work culture where energy is spent defending oneself rather than on productive activities. This environment can cause significant emotional stress for employees, reducing overall job satisfaction and increasing turnover rates.

最终，这会演变成互相归咎：以报复性指责、你一句我一句地甩锅为特征。它妨碍真正解决问题，恶化团队内部和跨部门之间的信任，让混乱更加根深蒂固。互相归咎会形成一种难以打破的负面循环，催生有毒的职场文化——大家把精力花在自我辩解上，而不是产出有价值的工作。这种环境会给员工带来巨大的情绪压力，拉低整体工作满意度，推高离职率。

— 原书第 24 页 —

High Turnover

高离职率

High turnover rates are a significant indicator of chaos. Employees leave due to burnout, dissatisfaction, and a lack of career development opportunities. This constant churn disrupts team cohesion and results in the loss of institutional knowledge.

高离职率是混乱的一个显著信号。员工因为倦怠、不满、看不到职业发展机会而离开。这种持续的人员流动会瓦解团队凝聚力，并造成组织经验的流失。

Frequent turnover can disrupt work continuity and increase recruitment and training costs. In addition, the loss of experienced employees can weaken the organization’s ability to maintain quality and consistency in its operations. High turnover also sends a negative signal to remaining employees and potential hires, damaging the organization’s reputation.

频繁的人员离职会打断工作连续性，推高招聘和培训成本。此外，资深员工的流失会削弱组织维持业务质量与一致性的能力。高离职率还会向留任员工和潜在候选人传递负面信号，损害组织的雇主声誉。

Lack of Strategy and Planning

缺乏战略与规划

Chaotic organizations often operate purely reactively, lacking clear strategy and planning. Teams and individuals frequently lack a clear sense of purpose or prioritization to guide their efforts. They respond to the latest fire drill rather than proactively working toward defined goals.

混乱的组织往往纯粹被动式运转，缺乏清晰的战略与规划。团队和个人常常没有明确的目标感或优先级来指引自己的努力，只是对最新冒出来的“救火”做出反应，而不是主动朝着既定目标推进。

Without strategic direction, effort is wasted on low-impact or even counterproductive activities. Resources aren’t optimally allocated because there is no clear prioritization of initiatives. The organization ends up frantically treading water rather than deliberately swimming toward a destination.

没有战略方向，努力就会浪费在低价值、甚至适得其反的事情上；由于没有清晰的优先级排序，资源也得不到最优配置。组织最终只是在拼命原地踩水，而不是有意识地朝某个目的地游去。

This disconnect between vision and implementation is also the primary driving force behind fissures between leadership and team members outside the engineering team. These fissures result in distrust and conflict between business units. A classic example is interactions between sales and engineering teams over what to sell and what is feasible to sell, with sales teams overselling and engineering teams overcommitting, undercommitting, or underdelivering.

愿景与执行之间的这种脱节，也是领导层与工程团队之外的成员之间产生裂痕的主要驱动力。这些裂痕会导致业务部门之间互不信任、冲突不断。一个典型例子就是销售与工程团队之间围绕“该卖什么、能卖什么”的拉扯：销售过度承诺，工程团队则要么承诺过头、要么承诺不足、要么交付不出来。

Frequent Crisis Mode

频繁陷入危机模式

Organizations in chaos often operate in a constant state of emergency. Every issue is treated as a crisis, which prevents strategic planning and leads to burnout. This mode of operation can also create a volatile work environment, where employees are constantly under stress. Living in a perpetual state of crisis can create a reactive rather than proactive culture. This environment can prevent the organization from focusing on long-term goals and improvements, as immediate issues consume all attention and resources, leaving little room for strategic planning and development. Chronic stress and burnout can lead to high absenteeism and increased turnover.

陷入混乱的组织常常处于一种持续的紧急状态。每个问题都被当成危机来处理，这让战略规划无从谈起，也导致倦怠。这种运转模式还会制造出一个动荡的工作环境，让员工始终处于压力之下。长期生活在危机状态中，会催生一种被动反应而非主动规划的文化。当眼前的问题耗尽了所有注意力和资源，组织就无暇聚焦长期目标和改进，几乎没有空间做战略规划与发展。慢性压力和倦怠还会导致高缺勤率和更高的离职率。

— 原书第 25 页 —

No Meaningful Measurement

缺乏有意义的度量

Finally, chaotic organizations often lack meaningful measurement. They don’t define or track metrics that provide a clear picture of the health and performance of the product, team, or business.

最后，混乱的组织往往缺乏有意义的度量。它们既不定义也不跟踪任何指标，无法清晰地看到产品、团队或业务的健康状况与表现。

Without data, it’s nearly impossible to spot problems, measure progress, or make informed decisions. Issues fester unnoticed until they blow up into major crises. Improvements or regressions happen without anyone understanding why. The organization is making decisions in the dark.

没有数据，几乎不可能发现问题、衡量进展或做出有依据的决策。问题在无人察觉中溃烂，直到爆发成重大危机。改进或退化发生了，却没人知道为什么。整个组织都在黑暗中做决策。

This lack of measurement makes it difficult to celebrate successes or learn from failures. There’s no reliable way to tell whether an initiative achieved its desired impact or to conduct a productive postmortem on an incident.

度量的缺失还让组织既难以庆祝成功，也难以从失败中学习。没有可靠的办法判断一项举措是否达成了预期效果，也无法对一次事故做有成效的复盘。

Chaos or Opportunity?

混乱还是机遇？

But there’s a flipside: chaos isn’t just something to survive—it’s where careers are made. Think about the most respected engineering leaders you know. Ask them about their defining moments. They won’t tell you about the time they maintained a stable system. They’ll tell you about inheriting a disaster, a team in freefall, or a product held together with duct tape. They became great by creating stability where none existed.

但事情还有另一面：混乱不只是熬过去就完了——它恰恰是成就职业生涯的地方。想想你认识的那些最受尊敬的工程领导者，问问他们人生中决定性的时刻是什么。他们不会跟你讲自己把一个稳定系统维护得多好，而会讲接手了一个烂摊子、一支自由落体般下坠的团队，或者一个全靠胶带粘着才没散架的产品。他们之所以变得优秀，正是因为在一无所有的地方亲手建起了稳定。

Chaos strips away bureaucracy. In established organizations, changing a deployment process requires committees, meetings, and PowerPoint decks that nobody reads. In chaos, you just fix it. If it works, that’s great; if not, try something else tomorrow. This is the paradox: the absence of structure becomes your permission to build. No ownership? Claim whatever you’re brave enough to own. No processes? You won’t fight six months to change “how we’ve always done things.” No metrics? You define success.

混乱会把官僚主义一层层剥掉。在成熟的组织里，改一个部署流程要经过委员会、会议和没人会读的 PPT；而在混乱里，你直接把它修好就行——成了最好，不成明天再试别的。这就是那个悖论：结构的缺失反而成了你动手搭建的许可。没人负责？那就去认领你敢于扛起的任何事。没有流程？你不必花半年去争取改变“我们一直以来的做法”。没有指标？那就由你来定义什么叫成功。

Undefined roles force you to develop range. You’re not just a backend engineer or team lead; you’re whatever the company needs that day. You learn product management by necessity. You figure out recruitment because someone has to. You understand business metrics because your engineering decisions suddenly have visible business impact.

模糊的角色会逼着你发展出多面手的能力。你不再只是一个后端工程师或团队负责人——你就是公司当天需要的任何角色。你出于必要学产品管理；因为总得有人干，你摸清了招聘；你的工程决策突然有了看得见的业务影响，于是你开始理解业务指标。

The lack of hierarchy creates unusual access. In chaos, you might find yourself explaining architecture changes directly to the chief executive officer. In other companies, that conversation filters through seven layers of management. Chaos collapses distance—your ideas reach decision makers immediately. But the most significant opportunity is this: chaos reveals who can build versus who can only maintain. The engineers who step up—who bring calm to storms, who ship when shipping seems impossible—are the ones who are remembered, promoted, and recruited. Additionally, when you inherit a mess, nobody expects miracles. Every small improvement is celebrated. (Compare that to taking over a high-performing team where the only direction is down.) In chaos, victories compound. Every fixed bug, every successful deployment, and every new hire who shows up will build momentum.

层级的缺失带来了不寻常的直达通道。在混乱中，你可能直接向 CEO 解释架构变更；而在另一些公司，同样的对话要过滤过七层管理层。混乱压缩了距离——你的想法能立刻到达决策者耳边。但最大的机遇在于：混乱会筛出谁真正能“建设”，谁只会“维护”。那些站出来的工程师——在风暴中带来冷静、在似乎不可能交付时仍然把东西发出去的人——才会被记住、被提拔、被争相挖角。而且，当你接手一个烂摊子时，没有人指望你创造奇迹，每一点小小的改进都会被庆祝一番。（对比一下接手一支高绩效团队吧，那边唯一的方向就是往下走。）在混乱中，胜利是会复利增长的：每修好一个 bug、每一次成功部署、每一个到岗的新同事，都在积累势能。

— 原书第 26 页 —

If you can find the eye of the hurricane and operate from there, chaos becomes your advantage. While others are frozen without structure, you’re building it. While they complain about the process, you ship solutions. The opportunity isn’t despite the dysfunction; it is because of it. Every missing piece is something essential that you can build. Every fire you extinguish increases your value. Every problem nobody else will touch becomes part of your leadership story.

如果你能找到飓风的风眼、在那里从容操作，混乱就会变成你的优势。当别人因没有结构而僵在原地时，你正在搭建结构；当他们在抱怨流程时，你已经把解决方案发了出去。机遇并不是“无视”功能失调而来的，恰恰是“因为”功能失调才存在的。每一块缺失的拼图，都是一件你可以亲手补上的关键之物；你扑灭的每一场火，都在提升你的价值；每个没人愿意碰的问题，都会成为你领导故事的一部分。

You’re not trying to eliminate all chaos; that’s impossible. You’re creating just enough order for productivity, just enough process to prevent disasters, just enough structure to maintain sanity. Companies that emerge strongest from chaos have leaders who understand this balance. They didn’t impose rigid order on fluid situations—they built systems that could bend without breaking.

你并不是要消灭所有混乱——那根本不可能。你要做的，是建立刚刚好的秩序让生产力运转起来，建立刚刚好的流程来防止灾难，建立刚刚好的结构让人不至于崩溃。那些从混乱中最强势地走出来的公司，都有懂得这种平衡的领导者：他们没有把僵硬的秩序强加于流变的局面，而是搭建了可以弯曲却不会断裂的系统。

Yes, chaos is indeed exhausting and stressful. But it’s also where reputations are built and leaders are forged. A year of successful leadership in chaos teaches more than five years of steady-state management. Once you see the opportunity hiding inside each problem, you’ll understand why some leaders actively seek chaotic environments. It’s not because they enjoy the suffering, but because that’s where there are opportunities to do fantastic work.

是的，混乱确实让人精疲力尽、压力山大。但也正是在这里，声誉被建立、领导者被锻造出来。在混乱中成功领导一年所学到的东西，胜过在稳态管理岗位上待五年。一旦你看穿每个问题背后藏着的机遇，就会理解为什么有些领导者会主动寻找混乱的环境——不是因为他们享受痛苦，而是因为那里才有机会做出了不起的工作。

Well, That Was Fun

好吧，这一趟不轻松

If any of those symptoms or the opportunities feel familiar, know you’re not alone. Chaos is the reality for many organizations, particularly during periods of rapid growth or significant change. These tumultuous times can exacerbate existing issues and create new ones, making it difficult to maintain order and efficiency. However, acknowledging the presence of chaos is the first step toward addressing it.

如果上面这些症状或机遇让你觉得“似曾相识”，请记住你并不孤单。混乱是许多组织的现实——尤其是在高速增长或重大变革时期。这些动荡的阶段会放大既有问题、制造新问题，让维持秩序与效率变得困难。但无论如何，承认混乱的存在，是着手解决它的第一步。

Chaos in an organization can be overwhelming, leading to frustration, decreased productivity, and high employee turnover. It can feel as if you’re constantly dealing with one crisis after another without making any real progress. This can be particularly challenging for leaders expected to steer the organization toward stability and success. The key to managing and overcoming chaos is recognizing these patterns early on and developing effective strategies to address them.

组织中的混乱可以让人喘不过气，带来挫败感、生产力下降和高离职率。你会感觉自己在一个接一个地处理危机，却始终没有真正的进展。对于那些被寄望于带领组织走向稳定与成功的领导者来说，这尤其艰难。应对并战胜混乱的关键，在于及早识别这些模式，并制定有效的策略去处理它们。

This involves thoroughly assessing the organization’s current state, identifying the root causes of chaos, and implementing targeted interventions to address these issues. It requires strong leadership, clear communication, and a commitment to continuous improvement.

这包括彻底评估组织的现状、找出混乱的根因，并实施有针对性的干预来解决这些问题。它需要强有力的领导、清晰的沟通，以及对持续改进的承诺。

— 原书第 27 页 —

This Sounds Scary

这听起来很可怕

We’d be remiss if we didn’t highlight that, after describing the many facets of chaotic organizations, sometimes the best solution is not working there at all. Throughout the book, we underscore the critical importance of self-care, maintaining good mental health, and prioritizing your safety and security. Working in and attempting to improve a chaotic organization is incredibly difficult, stressful, and emotionally draining. The constant flux and unpredictability can take a significant toll on your well-being, often leading to burnout and a sense of helplessness. Leadership, in its own right, is an isolating experience. The responsibility of guiding others, making tough decisions, and being the anchor for your team can create a unique form of loneliness. Leadership in a chaotic environment—where you may lack the support of leaders, peers, and mentors—is incredibly isolating. The absence of a reliable support system and the pressure to navigate through persistent instability will likely amplify feelings of isolation.

在把混乱组织的方方面面都讲完之后，如果我们不强调一点，那就是不负责任的：有时候，最好的解决方案根本就是别在那儿干。贯穿全书，我们都在强调自我照顾、保持良好心理健康、把自身安全与安稳放在首位的极端重要性。在一个混乱的组织里工作、并试图去改善它，是极其艰难、压力巨大、极度消耗情绪的事。持续的动荡和不可预测性会严重损害你的身心健康，常常导致倦怠和无助感。领导这件事本身就是一种孤独的体验：指引他人、做艰难决策、成为团队的锚，这些责任会带来一种独特的孤独。而在混乱环境中做领导——你可能得不到上级、同级和导师的支持——则孤独到了极点。缺乏可靠的支持系统，又要在持续的不稳定中独自掌舵，这些只会把孤立感放大。

We’ve both burnt out in roles where we felt overwhelmed and isolated. Our experiences have taught us that it’s vital to recognize when an environment is detrimental to your well-being and to have the courage to step away if necessary. It’s important to remember that no job is worth sacrificing your mental health or personal happiness over. Seeking healthier, more supportive work environments can lead to better professional outcomes and a more fulfilling, balanced life. Additionally, you must consider the long-term impact of staying in such an environment. Chronic stress and burnout can have severe consequences, including anxiety, depression, and other health issues.

我们俩都曾在那种让自己感到不堪重负、孤立无援的岗位上倦怠过。这些经历教会我们：认清一个环境是否正在损害你的身心健康至关重要；必要时，要有勇气抽身离开。请一定记住，没有任何一份工作值得你牺牲自己的心理健康或个人幸福。去寻找更健康、更有支持性的工作环境，往往会带来更好的职业结果，也会让生活更充实、更平衡。此外，你还必须考虑长期留在这种环境中的代价：慢性压力和倦怠可能造成严重后果，包括焦虑、抑郁以及其他健康问题。

When evaluating whether to stay or leave, consider your core values and long-term objectives. Ask yourself if the organization’s mission aligns with your personal and professional aspirations. Consider the growth opportunities, both personally and professionally. Are there mentors or leaders within the organization who can provide guidance and support? Is there a path forward that feels sustainable and fulfilling? If the answers to these questions are negative, it may be time to reassess your situation.

在去留之间做判断时，请想一想你的核心价值观和长期目标。问问自己：这家组织的使命，是否与你个人和职业上的抱负一致？这里有没有你在个人和专业上成长的空间？组织里有没有能给你指导和支持的导师或领导？有没有一条让你觉得可持续、有成就感的前进道路？如果这些问题的答案都是否定的，也许就到了重新评估自己处境的时候。

Finally, in the spirit of self-reflection, ask yourself, “Am I part of the problem too?” In addition to experiencing burnout and isolation, it’s easy to get caught up in the chaos and become a leader who enables or excuses it. Sometimes, in the name of defending your team, you may even become a toxic element in the organization. If you think this is you, consider whether you can change, whether your position is tenable if you try to make those changes, and whether it’s worth staying to make them at all.

最后，本着自我反思的精神，问自己一句：“我是不是也成了问题的一部分？”在经历倦怠和孤立之余，人很容易被卷进混乱，变成一个纵容、甚至为混乱找借口的领导。有时候，以“保护自己团队”为名，你自己反而成了组织里的一个有毒元素。如果你觉得这说的就是你，请认真想一想：你能否改变？如果你尝试去改变，自己的位置还坐不坐得住？以及，留下来做这些改变到底值不值得。

— 原书第 28 页 —

Moreover, building a solid support network outside of work is essential. Friends, family, and professional networks can provide the emotional support and perspective needed during challenging times. Activities that promote well-being—such as exercise, hobbies, and mindfulness practices—can serve as buffers against the stressors of a chaotic work environment.

此外，在工作之外建立一个稳固的支持网络也至关重要。朋友、家人和职业圈子，能在艰难时刻给你情感支撑和新的视角。那些促进身心健康的活动——比如锻炼、爱好、正念练习——可以缓冲混乱工作环境带来的压力。

Although the drive to improve and contribute to an organization is commendable, it’s equally important to recognize when the cost to your well-being is too high. Taking care of yourself should always be a priority. Leaving a chaotic organization is not a sign of failure but a step toward a healthier, more fulfilling professional life. Remember, you can choose environments that nurture and support your growth rather than diminish it. Prioritize your mental health, seek supportive work cultures, and don’t be afraid to make bold decisions in favor of your well-being.

虽然想要改善组织、为之贡献的劲头值得称道，但同样重要的是：要认清什么时候这个代价已经高到损害你的健康。照顾好自己永远应该是第一位的。离开一个混乱的组织，不是失败的标志，而是迈向更健康、更充实职业生活的一步。请记住，你可以选择那些滋养、支持你成长的环境，而不是消耗你的环境。把心理健康放在首位，去寻找有支持性的职场文化，并且不要害怕为了自己的福祉做出大胆的决定。

What Are We Going to Do to Help?

我们能帮上什么忙？

So, if you want to make a change in your organization, how will this book help you? We aim to equip you with principles, techniques, and mental models to help you lead effectively in chaotic environments. This book is designed to be a flexible toolkit that you can adapt to your specific context, recognizing that each organization and situation is unique. We offer a range of approaches that you can tailor to your specific needs, helping you address the unique challenges you face.

那么，如果你想在自己的组织里做出改变，这本书能帮到你什么？我们的目标是给你一套原则、技巧和心智模型，帮你在混乱的环境中有效领导。这本书被设计成一个灵活的工具箱，你可以根据自己的具体情境取用——毕竟每家组织、每种处境都是独特的。我们提供一系列方法，你可以按自己的需求裁剪，用来应对你面前那些独一无二的挑战。

Throughout the book, we explore various topics that are crucial for engineering leaders in fast-paced, growing, and chaotic companies. We discuss the importance of embracing the unknown, navigating minimal structure, and understanding the multifaceted roles and responsibilities of an engineering leader. You’ll learn core leadership skills, including adaptability, effective communication, business and product acumen, empathy, collaboration, and strategic thinking.

全书会探讨一系列对快节奏、增长中、混乱中的公司里的工程领导者至关重要的话题。我们会讨论拥抱未知、在极简结构中航行，以及理解工程领导者多面角色与责任的重要性。你将学到核心的领导技能，包括适应力、高效沟通、业务与产品敏感度、同理心、协作和战略思考。

Next, we will explore how to set direction, build cohesive teams, and scale through systems and delegation. You’ll learn to establish goals, develop strategies, align company objectives with team goals, build capable teams, celebrate successes, avoid burnout, and leverage external support. We also discuss implementing efficient systems and empowering teams while managing dependencies.

接下来，我们会探讨如何设定方向、打造有凝聚力的团队，并通过系统和授权来实现规模化。你将学习如何制定目标、设计战略、把公司目标与团队目标对齐、搭建有能力的团队、庆祝成功、避免倦怠，以及利用外部支持。我们还会讨论如何落地高效的系统、在管理好依赖关系的同时赋能团队。

The next chapters tackle the challenges of managing technical and operational chaos. You’ll learn various prioritization techniques, how to balance different types of work (features, technical debt, and maintenance), and how to plan and budget effectively, including vendor management and procurement. We also focus on technical strategy and execution, covering topics such as aligning technical strategy with business goals, setting and implementing technical principles, addressing scaling challenges, making informed decisions about new technologies, and fostering collaborative technical practices and decision making.

后续章节会处理管理技术与运营混乱的挑战。你会学到各种优先级排序技巧、如何在不同类型的工作（新功能、技术债、维护）之间取得平衡，以及如何有效地做规划和预算，包括供应商管理与采购。我们还会聚焦技术战略与执行，话题涵盖：让技术战略与业务目标对齐、制定并落地技术原则、应对规模化挑战、在新技术上做出有依据的决策，以及培育协作式的技术实践与技术决策方式。

— 原书第 29 页 —

We emphasize the importance of using metrics for continuous improvement, introducing you to some useful metrics and teaching you how to apply them to assess organizational performance. You’ll also learn how to develop capabilities to measure, test, and accelerate innovation through continuous experimentation, observability, comprehensive testing strategies, and balancing quantitative and qualitative feedback.

我们会强调用指标驱动持续改进的重要性，向你介绍一些实用指标，并教你如何用它们评估组织表现。你还将学习如何培养相应能力，通过持续实验、可观测性、全面的测试策略，以及平衡定量与定性反馈，来度量、检验并加速创新。

Throughout the book, we share real examples from our experiences, along with actionable tips and practices you can try. These examples will provide concrete illustrations of the concepts discussed, making them more relatable and accessible. By the end, you’ll feel more confident and capable of leading through the chaos, equipped with practical strategies and insights that you can implement immediately.

全书我们都会分享亲身经历中的真实案例，以及你可以立刻上手的可操作建议和做法。这些案例会让书中的概念变得具体、可感、容易理解。读完之后，你会更有信心、更有能力带领团队穿越混乱，手里握着可以立刻落地的实用策略与洞见。

You can’t control the whole organization, but you can start building capabilities designed to enhance control and improve the situation. By focusing on what you can influence directly, you can create pockets of stability and efficiency that can serve as models for the rest of the organization. This approach enhances your immediate environment and demonstrates the effectiveness of your methods, potentially inspiring broader organizational change.

你无法控制整个组织，但你可以从建立能力开始，一步步增强掌控感、改善处境。把注意力放在你能直接影响的事情上，你就能创造出一片片稳定而高效的“飞地”，让它们成为组织其他部分的样板。这种做法既能改善你眼前的小环境，又能证明你这套方法的有效性，甚至可能激发更大范围的组织变革。

The book also includes appendices and resources, such as additional tools, exercises, extended reading, reference materials, and case studies to further your learning and application of the presented concepts.

本书还包含附录和延伸资源，比如额外的工具、练习、延伸阅读、参考材料和案例研究，帮助你进一步学习和应用书中的概念。

The most successful engineering leaders we know didn’t succeed despite the chaos; they succeeded because of it. Chaos strips away pretense, accelerates learning, and rewards those who can create order from disorder. While established companies debate decisions in committees for months, you can implement solutions in days. While they manage politics, you solve real problems. While they protect the status quo, you build the future.

我们认识的最成功的工程领导者，并不是“顶着混乱”取得成功的，而是“借着混乱”成功的。混乱会剥去伪装、加速学习，并奖励那些能从无序中建立秩序的人。当成熟公司还在委员会里为一个决策争论几个月时，你几天之内就能把方案落地；当他们在经营办公室政治时，你在解决真实的问题；当他们在维护现状时，你在建造未来。

By synthesizing the skills and strategies covered throughout the book and engaging in practical applications through simulated projects and real-world scenarios, you’ll learn how to effectively lead in chaotic environments and drive success for your team and organization.

通过把全书的技能与策略融会贯通，并在模拟项目和真实场景中加以实践，你将学会如何在混乱的环境中有效领导，并为你的团队和组织驱动成功。

Conclusion: From Chaos to Clarity

结语：从混乱到清晰

You’ve seen the symptoms: a lack of ownership, constant firefighting, a blame culture, and teams shipping code without understanding what and why they are shipping. You may have recognized your own organization in these descriptions. Maybe you’re feeling overwhelmed by the scale of dysfunction that you’re facing. Here’s the reality: you can’t fix everything. The chaos won’t magically disappear because you’ve identified it. But you can control your own approach to leadership—and that starts with getting clear on what your job actually is.

你已经看到了这些症状：缺乏主人翁意识、永远在救火、指责文化，以及团队在并不清楚自己在交付什么、为什么交付的情况下就把代码发了出去。你可能在这些描述里认出了自己的组织，也可能正被眼前功能失调的规模压得喘不过气。现实是：你无法修好一切。混乱不会因为你识别出了它就神奇消失。但你可以掌控自己的领导方式——而这，要从弄清楚你的工作到底是什么开始。

— 原书第 30 页 —

Most engineering leaders in chaotic environments fail because they try to do everything at once. They juggle fixing processes, mentoring engineers, managing emergencies, and setting strategy, all without a fundamental framework for their role. They end up exhausted and ineffective, contributing to the very chaos they’re trying to solve.

混乱环境中，大多数工程领导者之所以失败，是因为他们试图一次性把所有事都做了：一边修流程、一边辅导工程师、一边处理紧急事故、一边定战略，却唯独没有一个关于自己角色的根本框架。结果他们既疲惫又低效，反而成了自己想解决的那个混乱的一部分。

The alternative is to focus on five core pillars that define engineering leadership:

另一条路，是聚焦于定义工程领导力的五大核心支柱：

  • People. Building and developing your team, from hiring to performance management to creating a collaborative culture

    人（People）。建设并发展你的团队——从招聘、绩效管理，到打造协作文化。

  • Mission. Connecting your engineers to the “why” behind their work, even when company direction is unclear

    使命（Mission）。哪怕公司方向尚不清晰，也要把工程师与他们工作背后的“为什么”连接起来。

  • Plan. Creating roadmaps and priorities that balance business needs with technical reality

    计划（Plan）。制定路线图与优先级，在业务需求和技术现实之间取得平衡。

  • Process. Establishing workflows that enable rather than obstruct, keeping things lightweight but effective

    流程（Process）。建立“赋能而非阻碍”的工作流，保持轻量却有效。

  • Product. Ensuring your team delivers outcomes that matter, not just output that looks good on a dashboard

    产品（Product）。确保你的团队交付的是有价值的结果，而不只是仪表盘上好看的产出。

These aren’t abstract concepts; they’re the practical foundations of your role. Get these right, and you create stability in your immediate sphere of influence. That stability then becomes a model for the broader organization.

这些不是抽象概念，而是你这个角色的现实根基。把这五件事做对，你就能在自己直接影响的范围内建立稳定；而这份稳定，又会成为更大范围组织的样板。

In Chapter 2, we’ll work through each pillar systematically. You’ll assess where you are, define where you need to be, and create a concrete role description that reflects your actual responsibilities (not the generic job posting that got you hired). This isn’t about creating more bureaucracy—it’s about giving yourself a framework to operate from when everything else is in flux.

在第 2 章，我们会系统地逐一拆解这五大支柱。你将评估自己现在所处的位置、定义自己需要到达的位置，并写出一份反映你真实职责的具体角色说明（而不是当年把你招进来的那份通用 JD）。这不是为了制造更多官僚主义——而是为了在其他一切都变动不居时，给自己一个可以立足行事的框架。

The chaos will still be there tomorrow. But at least you’ll know what you’re responsible for and how to approach it. Sometimes that’s enough to get started.

明天混乱依然会在那里。但至少你会清楚自己该为什么负责、以及该如何入手。有时候，这就足以让你迈出第一步了。
